title: Predictable capacity sourcing: procurement storyline and sales play
content:
Executive summary

Draft storyline to use in procurement conversations where buyers ask for predictable throughput and guarantees. Goal: give sales a concise narrative plus objection handling, negotiation levers, and a procurement-ready appendix they can drop into an SOW. This is intentionally pragmatic and abbreviated — use it as a script and modify per account.

Core positioning (elevator):
- Redwood Dedicated gives predictable inference capacity with contractual throughput guarantees, physical isolation of tenant GPU pools, and built-in graceful degradation. Customers get the economics of managed inference with the operational predictability of reserved capacity.

Value pillars to emphasize (single-sentence hooks):
1) Predictable unit economics: reserved pools + commitment pricing reduces per-token cost and eliminates sudden bill spikes when traffic grows.
2) Deterministic performance: p95/p99 latency and sustained throughput guarantees backed by capacity commitments and autoscaling policies.
3) Isolation & compliance: dedicated GPU pools and private networking ensure customer workloads are not impacted by noisy neighbors; integrates with KMS and audit logging for regulated use cases.
4) Operational simplicity: same Redwood API and tooling across hosted/dedicated/private — no heavy migration of code or retraining of ops teams.

Common procurement asks and tight rebuttals (concise):
- "We can run models ourselves cheaper." -> Rebuttal: baseline TCO often understates ops and engineering costs: model upgrades, kernel tuning, batching knobs, and reliability engineering. We bake in runtime optimizations and observability that reduce engineering burden; supplemented with a predictable committed price. Offer to run an apples-to-apples TCO calc during pilot.
- "What happens during high demand?" -> Rebuttal: Contracted throughput is isolated; for headroom buys we propose a burst bucket and automated fallback to compatible model variants. Show the fallback / degrade flow and SLA credit policy.
- "How do you define SLA?" -> Rebuttal: Use simple measurable targets (availability %, throughput units delivered, p99 latency) and attach credits tied to those metrics. Provide examples below.
- "How will we test it?" -> Rebuttal: We provide a joint performance validation plan — synthetic load tests using your prompt mix plus a short pilot (1–2 weeks) to validate the profile and confirm measurement.

Procurement-ready SLA sketch (example clauses to copy):
- Service Commitment: Redwood will make Dedicated Capacity available with a monthly committed throughput of X throughput units (TU).
- Measurement: Throughput units will be counted per successful request (definition: 1 TU = 1 1k-token request normalized) and measured via Redwood telemetry.
- Availability Target: Monthly Uptime of service-hosting endpoints >= 99.95%.
- Latency Targets: p95 < 350ms, p99 < 750ms for requests within the committed TU profile.
- Isolation Guarantee: Customer workloads will be served from isolated GPU pools and network boundaries that exclude third-party tenant workloads.
- Remedies: For each 0.1% below availability target, customer will receive a 3% credit of the monthly committed fee, up to 30%. Credits do not apply for scheduled maintenance or force majeure.
- Scaling Fallbacks: During temporary capacity constraints Redwood will notify customer and automatically route non-committed traffic to compatible hosted variants with degradation policy; committed TU traffic remains prioritized.

Negotiation levers (what sales can offer without engineering churn):
- Minimum commitment tiers (monthly TU bands) and a short-term pilot band with conversion discounts.
- Burst credits for seasonal spikes (pre-purchased or on-demand with short notice).
- Enhanced telemetry retention and custom dashboards as an add-on (low marginal cost).
- Uptime SLA vs price: small tradeoffs in credits vs reduced committed price.
- Migration assistance credits (1–2 weeks of engineering time) for larger migrations.

Customer objections that require product/eng decisions (flag these):
- Fine-grained isolation (dedicated PCI-e-attached devices vs. tenant-separated VMs): requires security/infrastructure review.
- On-prem appliance footprint: needs product packaging & ops checklist.
- Custom model artifact residency rules: legal + infra review.

Technical hook bullets (for technical buyers):
- Kernel and compilation selection tuned per customer workload to maximize throughput at target sequence lengths.
- Prefix and KV caching: reduces per-token compute for repeated conversational patterns.
- Request routing policies by latency/cost/region to honor locality SLOs without changing API.
- Autoscaling policies that maintain guaranteed throughput while minimizing idle cost through warm-pool and burst buckets.

Competitive differentiation (how to position vs alternatives):
- Vs. hyperscale cloud-managed inference: Hyperscalers offer scale but often mix tenants. We deliver isolation guarantees and a transparent cost/perf model tuned for LLM use cases (prefix cache, continuous batching).
- Vs. self-hosted open-source stacks: Self-hosting gives control but hidden ops burden and slower time-to-market. Redwood couples high-performance runtime optimizations with managed operations and predictable economics.
- Vs. other LLM API vendors: Emphasize the SLO-first approach (contracted throughput + isolation) and the tooling for observability and rollouts that reduce risk during model upgrades.

Deck / sales script snippets (short bullets for slides or call notes):
- Slide: "Predictable inference for product teams" — one-liner + 3 icons: Cost, SLAs, Isolation.
- Script: "We treat throughput like a product feature — you'll get a committed pool, a fallback plan, and a single-pane view into usage and latency."
- Slide: "How downtime costs translate to your business" — simple table mapping 10% traffic loss to revenue/UX impacts.
- Script: use customer example: "Customer X moved high-value flows to Dedicated and reduced incident MTTR from 3 hours to 12 minutes; they cut per-token cost 23% after tuning." (swap with live customer metrics).

Validation plan (pilot -> scale):
1) Kickoff: agree on evaluation prompts and success criteria (SLOs + cost).
2) Synthetic perf pass: Redwood runs load tests with customer's prompt distribution to size pool.
3) Short prod pilot (2–4 weeks): live traffic under limited routing, validate metrics and costs.
4) Ramp & cutover: phased routing of traffic, runbook and rollback hooks.
5) Post-mortem + quality/regression check.

Pricing constructs to propose (examples):
- Committed TU + per-TU overage at smaller premium.
- Committed TU + burst bucket (purchased or short-term rental).
- Multi-year commit discounts and optional usage true-up.

Appendix: sample measurement definitions (so procurement doesn't ask ambiguous questions):
- TU definition: unitized per-1k tokens processed, normalized across model families using benchmarking profiles.
- Successful request: returned response with 2xx status code and < 10s end-to-end time measured at Redwood edge.
- Measurement window: hourly windows aggregated to monthly for SLO calculations.

Plain-language FAQ (for field use):
- "Is our data co-mingled?" -> No. Dedicated GPU pools + optional Private control plane keeps data isolated; encryption at rest + KMS.
- "Can we get credits if you miss the SLA?" -> Yes — credits scale with shortfalls; we include a cap and carve-outs for scheduled maintenance.
- "How quickly can we scale capacity?" -> Within committed tiers: immediate. Beyond committed tiers: subject to regional capacity, typically 24–72 hours for large allocations.

Open questions / TO-DOs (items for product or legal to finalize):
- Finalize TU normalization approach for mixed-model fleets (action: eng + applied-ml to produce benchmark table).
- Confirm maximum credit cap and exclusion list for force majeure events (action: legal).
- Create a short one-page SOW insert for sales (action: legal + GTM ops).
- Prepare a 2-slide technical appendix for sales engineers illustrating fallback flow and cache behavior.

Next steps for field:
- Sales to trial script with two pilot accounts this quarter.
- Se-team: build quick TCO workbook template to compare committed vs. self-hosted.
- Product: deliver benchmark artifacts for TU normalization (ETA 3 weeks).

Notes to self (raw):
- Keep credit math simple and predictable; procurement hates opaque formulas.
- Don't overpromise latency numbers for long-tail requests (rare 2–5s cases). Flag long-tail SLA carve-outs.
- Use examples and customer stories when possible — make it concrete.

End of draft.

(Version notes: first sketch tailored for sales training. Will iterate with legal and eng before publishing as a canonical playbook.)
